name: Single-breasted suit

card.summary: The single-breasted suit is the standard one-column-of-buttons suit, and a well-fitted one sharpens shoulders, defines the waist and lengthens the torso line.

quick.overview:
A single-breasted suit jacket closes with a single column of buttons, usually two or three, with the front panels meeting at the centre of the torso. It is the most common suit cut and the default business and formal option.

Its appearance payoff comes from fit and proportion. Button position affects how tall and balanced the wearer looks, and a jacket that follows the shoulders and waist creates a clean silhouette.
quick.how: People wear it with the top button or buttons fastened and the bottom button open, as the cut intends, and typically unbutton when seated. Tailoring to the shoulders, sleeve and jacket length is the usual way to get the look. It pairs with a shirt and tie or an open collar depending on the occasion.
quick.risks: There are no health risks; the practical downsides are cost, and that an ill-fitting jacket can make the frame look boxier or shorter. Button placement that sits too low is described as drawing the eye downward and making the waist look larger.

lead: A single-breasted suit has one column of buttons down the front, and the jacket's two sides meet at the centre of the torso, overlapping enough to close one to three buttons [1]. Two or three buttons is typical; four or more is unusual, and dinner jackets commonly have one [1]. By convention the lowest button is cut so that it does not close [1].

For people trying to improve their appearance, the suit is a way to shape the body's outline: structure at the shoulder, a defined waist and a longer vertical line. Wikipedia notes that button height influences perceived height, with buttons set too low or a strongly rolling lapel pulling the eye downward and making the waist look larger [1].
It differs from the double-breasted suit, which has two columns of buttons and a large front overlap and is usually kept buttoned [1].

chain: Tailored shoulders and a defined waist
angle.text: A well-fitted single-breasted jacket shapes the silhouette, with button position and lapel shape affecting how tall and balanced the wearer looks. It is the usual default suit for formal and work settings.

paras: The jacket's fronts overlap just enough to fasten, in contrast with the double-breasted design [1]. Convention is to leave the lowest button open, and wearers generally unbutton the jacket when seated to avoid awkward drape [1].

The single-breasted peaked-lapel jacket was popular in the late 1920s and 1930s and returned in the 1970s, according to Wikipedia [1]. Double-breasted suits of the 1980s were associated with power dressing [1].

Canvas construction gives a balanced silhouette so that the jacket hangs well buttoned or open [1]. Button height is said to shape perceived height, so lower buttons can shorten the look of the torso [1].
Style advice on T Nation threads about dressing for a funeral favoured a black suit with no accessories apart from an understated watch, showing the suit's role as a default formal choice [2].
